title: Three HD 303514 mass-ratio states retain both eclipses through 2060 under the published equal-radius light model
abstract: We test the inner equal-mass assumption in the HD 303514 near-coplanar recovery model. We use 44 published TESS and ASAS-3 timing and shape constraints, full Newtonian integrations, and 1,490 DASCH DR7 plates excluded from the orbit fit. The inner total mass is fixed at four solar masses and the published equal-radius light model is retained. At inner mass ratios 0.5, 1 and 2, the attained costs are 51.434, 46.884 and 50.090, with third-star masses of 2.672, 2.010 and 2.442 solar masses. The ratio-2 search reaches its 40-evaluation limit; its cost is not an established minimum. All three states retain both eclipses through 2060, with minimum depths near 2030-2035. The smallest separation margin is only 0.025 stellar radii. Common-shape plate timing gains are 68.69, 80.38 and 67.95, favoring the equal-mass state within this finite comparison. At that state, other fitted parameters absorb more than 99.65 percent of the squared local mass-ratio response. A derivative stability test and retarded-position checks are included. Free plate amplitudes require a separate physical color model. These results are a conditional assumption test, not a measured inner mass ratio, a new mass interval, or an eclipse-loss probability. Limits include fixed radii and mass scale, inherited correlated estimates, local searches, and plate calibration and time errors.

display.caption: Three tested states under equal-radius light constraints. Lines connect attained states; they are not a confidence profile. The q = 2 search reached its iteration limit. The plate amplitude is free and is not linked to a stellar color model.

Conditional conjunction separations. Contact is lost at 2 R for equal stellar radii. All modeled eclipses through 2060 retain contact in these three states. Fixed radii and the finite orbit search limit this result.
Model timing differences from the equal-mass state at matched inner cycles. The gray area marks the modern interval. These curves are simulated histories, not newly measured plate eclipse times.
